'''Lewis Robert Goldberg''' (January 28, 1932 – March 29, 2026) was an American personality psychologist and academic who was a professor emeritus at the [[University of Oregon]]. He was closely associated<ref name="Goldberg93">{{Cite journal |last=Goldberg |first=Lewis R. |date=1993 |title=The structure of phenotypic personality traits. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0003-066X.48.1.26 |journal=American Psychologist |language=en |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=26–34 |doi=10.1037/0003-066X.48.1.26 |issn=1935-990X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> with the [[lexical hypothesis]] that any culturally important personality characteristic will be represented in the language of that culture. This hypothesis led to a five factor structure of personality trait adjectives (which he dubbed the [[Big Five personality traits|Big 5]]).<ref name="big5">{{Cite journal |last=Goldberg |first=Lewis R. |date=1990 |title=An alternative "description of personality": The Big-Five factor structure. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0022-3514.59.6.1216 |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=59 |issue=6 |pages=1216–1229 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.59.6.1216 |issn=1939-1315|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="sanjay">{{Cite web |url=https://www.uoregon.edu/~sanjay/bigfive.html |title=Measuring the Big Five Personality Factors |access-date=2010-03-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100209071733/http://www.uoregon.edu/~sanjay/bigfive.html |archive-date=2010-02-09 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="bill">{{Citation |chapter=Goldberg, Lewis R. (1932-) |date=2008 |title=Encyclopedia of Counseling |chapter-url=https://sk.sagepub.com/ency/edvol/counseling/chpt/goldberg-lewis-r-1932 |access-date=2026-01-05 |location=Thousand Oaks California |publisher=SAGE Publications, Inc. |doi=10.4135/9781412963978.n198 |isbn=978-1-4129-0928-0|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>  When applied to personality items this structure is also known as the  [[Big Five personality traits|five-factor model (FFM)]] of [[personality]].  He is the creator of the [[International Personality Item Pool]]<ref name="IPIP1">https://ipip.ori.org/</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://ipip.ori.org/A%20broad-bandwidth%20inventory.pdf|author1=Lewis R. Goldberg|year=1999|title=A broad-bandwidth, public domain, personality inventory measuring the lower-level facets of several five-factor models. |editor=Mervielde, I. |editor2=Deary, I. |editor3=De Fruyt, F. |editor4=Ostendorf, F.|journal=Personality Psychology in Europe|volume=7|pages=7–28}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Goldberg, Lewis R.|author2=Johnson, John A|author3=Eber, Herbert W.|author4=Hogan, Robert|author5=Ashton, Michael C.|author6=Clonginger, C. Robert|author7=Gough, Harrison G.|title=The international personality item pool and the future of public-domain personality measures|journal=Journal of Research in Personality|date=2006|volume=40|issue=1|pages=84–96|doi=10.1016/j.jrp.2005.08.007|s2cid=13274640 }}</ref>(IPIP),<ref name="goldbergL" /> a website that provides public-domain personality measures.

==Early life and education==
Lewis Robert Goldberg was born in [[Chicago, Illinois]] on January 28, 1932. His early education took place at the Bret Harte elementary school in Chicago, and the Highland Park High School in Highland Park, Illinois. In 1953 Goldberg received an A.B. in social relations from [[Harvard University]]. He earned a Ph.D. in psychology from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1958 where his Ph.D. advisor was [[E. Lowell Kelly]]; Kelly provided Goldberg with training in the methodology of quantitative personality assessment.<ref name="bill" /><ref name="goldbergL" />

==Academic career==
As an advanced graduate student at Michigan, Goldberg met [[Warren Norman (psychologist)|Warren T Norman]], a new assistant professor, who became a lifelong friend and collaborator on issues in personality structure and assessment.  Their initial work together on the generality of the Big 5, and their subsequent work on the [[lexical hypothesis]] has had a major impact upon the development of a consensual  model of personality.  After receiving his doctorate, Goldberg became a visiting assistant professor at [[Stanford University]]. Since 1960 he has taught at the [[University of Oregon]], where he is professor emeritus.<ref name="goldbergL">{{cite web |url=https://www.ori.org/Research/scientists/goldbergL.html |title=Lewis R. Goldberg, Ph.D. |accessdate=2006-01-25 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20060202181319/http://www.ori.org/Research/scientists/goldbergL.html |archivedate=2006-02-02 }}</ref> He is a senior scientist at the [[Oregon Research Institute]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=ORI {{!}} Advancing science. Enhancing lives. |url=https://www.ori.org/ |access-date=2026-01-05 |language=en-US}}</ref> where he has carried out research since 1961.<ref name="goldbergL" />

From 1962 to 1966, Goldberg served as a field selection officer for the  United States [[Peace Corps]]. In 1966 he became a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright]] professor at the [[Radboud University Nijmegen|University of Nijmegen]], the Netherlands. In 1970 he spent a year as a visiting professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name="goldbergL" />

In 1974 he was a Fulbright professor again, at [[Istanbul University]] in Turkey.<ref name="goldbergL" /> From 1980 to 1986 he served as a consultant in the Intelligence Division of the [[United States Secret Service]]. He was a fellow at the [[Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study]] from 1981 to 1982.<ref name="goldbergL" />

Goldberg published more than 150 research articles.<ref name="goldbergL" />  He has also earned three lifetime achievement awards: the [[Jack Block]] Award for outstanding contributions to personality research from the [[Society for Personality and Social Psychology]] (SPSP) (2006), the Saul Sells Award for outstanding contributions to multivariate research from the [[Society of Multivariate Experimental Psychology]] (SMEP) (2006), and most recently the [[Bruno Klopfer]] Award for outstanding contributions to personality assessment from the Society for Personality Assessment (SPA) (2009).<ref name="goldbergL" />

==Personality structure and measurement==
Throughout his career, Goldberg has made substantial contributions to the [[measurement of personality]].  His early work<ref name="big5"/> examined the multidimensional structure of adjectival descriptors sampled from prior lexical work of Norman.  This was an important contribution suggesting that the "Big Five" factors of peer ratings could be identified in adjectives representing a sample of the lexicon.  Subsequent work on the [[lexical hypothesis]], in collaboration with two prominent Dutch scholars, suggested that the structure could be seen as a set of circumplexes embedded in five dimensional spaces.<ref>Hofstee, Willem K. and de Raad, Boele and Goldberg, Lewis R. (1992), Integration of the Big Five and circumplex approaches to trait structure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 63, 143-163</ref> Goldberg also did a study on act-frequency signatures of the “Big Five” and how much in our incidental or everyday behavior that we show signature behavior pertaining to the “Big Five.” These five aspects showed up numerous times during the reported study and this shows that we exhibit behavioral signatures of the “Big Five,” those being extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability, and intellect. This is important as Goldberg's research may help enrich our understanding of our everyday mundane actions and how our personality affects it.<ref>Chapman, B. P., & Goldberg, L. R. (2017). Act-frequency signatures of the Big Five. ''Personality and Individual Differences'', ''116'', 201–205. <nowiki>https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2017.04.049</nowiki></ref>

Goldberg and his colleagues later released the [[International Personality Item Pool]],<ref name="IPIP1"/> which is an international "Collaboratory" which contains more than 3,000 short item stems summarizing the content of many personality inventories. At least 250 separate scales have been developed from the IPIP items, and at least some of the items have been translated into more than 35 languages.  Validity data for these scales comes from a longitudinal sample of approximately 800 community volunteers in the cities of [[Eugene, Oregon|Eugene]] and [[Springfield, Oregon|Springfield]] in [[Oregon]]. These participants have taken the IPIP items as well as proprietary instruments measuring temperamental traits, occupational interests, and various activities. Goldberg, in his typically open spirit  of collaborative science, provides the data from the Eugene-Springfield sample to interested researchers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lim |first1=Beng-Chong |last2=Ployhart |first2=Robert E. |date=January 2006 |title=Assessing the Convergent and Discriminant Validity of Goldberg's International Personality Item Pool: A Multitrait-Multimethod Examination |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1094428105283193 |journal=Organizational Research Methods |language=en |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=29–54 |doi=10.1177/1094428105283193 |issn=1094-4281|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Personality consistency over the lifespan==
With his colleague Sarah Hampson, Goldberg initiated a 40-year follow up to a study started by [[John Digman]] at the University of Hawaii.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hampson |first=Sarah E. |last2=Goldberg |first2=Lewis R. |date=October 2006 |title=A first large cohort study of personality trait stability over the 40 years between elementary school and midlife. |url=https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.91.4.763 |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |volume=91 |issue=4 |pages=763–779 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.91.4.763 |issn=1939-1315 |pmc=2247365 |pmid=17014298}}</ref>  This study is examining the health outcomes in middle adulthood associated with personality rating in middle school.

==Personality and prediction==
Goldberg's early work compared clinical versus actuarial prediction.  Even when predicting clinically difficult criteria, he showed that actuarial models were superior to clinical judgment.<ref>L.R. Goldberg,(1970) Man versus model of man:a rationale, plus some evidence, for a method of improving on clinical inference.  Psychological Bulletin, 72, (6) p 422-432.</ref>

==Other major publications==
Besides his articles discussing the dimensions of personality, Goldberg has also contributed to the studies showing the importance of personality for predicting important life outcomes with his colleagues [[Brent Roberts]], Nathan Kuncel, Rebecca Shiner and [[Avshalom Caspi]].<ref>BW Roberts, NR Kuncel, R Shiner, A Caspi, LR Goldberg  The power of personality: The comparative validity of personality traits, socioeconomic status, and cognitive ability for predicting important life outcomes, Perspectives on Psychological science. 2 (4), 313-345</ref>

His methodological papers includes the development of the "bass-ackwards" procedure for assessing hierarchical structures.<ref>LR Goldberg. Doing it all bass-ackwards: The development of hierarchical factor structures from the top down. Journal of Research in Personality 40 (4), 347-358</ref> as well as his careful comparison of multiple ways to form personality scales for prediction.<ref>LR Goldberg  Parameters of personality inventory construction and utilization: A comparison of prediction strategies and tactics. Multivariate Behavioral Research Monographs. 1972.</ref>

==Boards and committees==
Goldberg served on the Personality and Cognition Research Review Committee and the Cognition, Emotion, and Personality Research Review Committee of the [[National Institute of Mental Health]] and on the [[Graduate Record Examination]] Board Research Committee.<ref name="goldbergL" /> Goldberg has previously served as the president of the [[Society of Multivariate Experimental Psychology]] (1974–1975) the [[Association for Research in Personality]] (2004–2006) and [[The World Association for Personality Psychology]] (2019–2024). He is a fellow of the [[American Psychological Association]], the [[Association for Psychological Science]], and the [[Society for Personality and Social Psychology]].

==Death==
Goldberg died on March 29, 2026, at the age of 94.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lewis R. Goldberg, Ph.D., – In Memorium |url=https://www.ori.org/project/goldberg-lew/ |website=ORI |access-date=18 May 2026}}</ref>
